# Το Τελευταίο Καλοκαίρι

Κάθονταν στα σκαλιά της παραλίας, με τα πόδια τους να αγγίζουν την άμμο. Ο Θανάσης κοιτούσε τη θάλασσα σαν να έψαχνε εκεί μέσα κάποια απάντηση.

«Χίλια χιλιόμετρα», είπε τελικά.

«Χίλια εκατόν είκοσι», τον διόρθωσε η Σοφία με ένα μισό χαμόγελο. «Τα μέτρησα».

Γέλασε. Φυσικά τα είχε μετρήσει. Αυτή που θα πήγαινε να μάθει στα μικρά παιδιά τον κόσμο, ενώ εκείνος θα έλυνε εξισώσεις στο άλλο άκρο της χώρας.

Της έπιασε το χέρι.

«Υπάρχει λύση», είπε εκείνος.

«Σε κάθε πρόβλημα;» ρώτησε εκείνη.

«Σε κάθε πρόβλημα».

Δεν ήξεραν αν αυτό ήταν αλήθεια. Αλλά το καλοκαίρι ήταν ακόμα εκεί, ολόκληρο μπροστά τους, και για την ώρα αρκούσε.

Stavros and Georgia stood in the hospital corridor, speaking in hushed voices while their father sat beside their mother's bed, holding her hand.

"A month," Georgia whispered, rubbing her temples. "At least."

"I know," Stavros said.

They both stared at the floor. Georgia had a new job she had barely started. Stavros had a project at work that his boss had been planning for six months.

Neither of them spoke for a long moment.

"Coin toss," Stavros finally said, pulling a euro from his pocket.

Georgia looked at him, then nodded slowly. "Fine. Heads I stay, tails you stay."

The coin spun in the air, caught the fluorescent light, and landed in Stavros's palm. He slapped it onto the back of his hand and lifted his fingers.

Tails.

He stared at it for a moment, then closed his fist around the coin and put it back in his pocket.

"I'll call my boss in the morning," he said quietly.

Georgia touched his arm. "I'll come every weekend. I promise."

He nodded and pushed open the door to their mother's room. She looked small in the white bed, but she smiled when she saw him.

That made it easier.

# The Coin Toss

Georgia and Stavros stood in the hospital hallway while their father slept, his leg wrapped in a thick white cast.

"One of us has to stay," Georgia said quietly.

Stavros nodded, staring at his shoes. He had a new job starting Monday. Georgia had her final university exams next week.

Neither spoke for a moment.

"Flip a coin," Stavros finally said, pulling one from his pocket.

"That's how we're deciding this?" Georgia raised an eyebrow.

"You have a better idea?"

She didn't.

The coin spun in the air. It landed on the floor and rolled under a chair.

They both looked at each other, then burst out laughing — the kind of tired, helpless laughter that only family can share.

"I'll stay," Georgia said, catching her breath. "My professors will understand. Your boss won't."

Stavros grabbed her hand. "I'll come every weekend. I'll bring food, I'll clean, I'll—"

"You'll call Mama every single day," she interrupted firmly.

"Every single day," he promised.

She walked back into their father's room, pulled up a chair beside his bed, and stayed.
